title: Multisensory, Nature-Inspired Recharge Rooms Yield Short-Term Reductions in Perceived Stress Among Frontline Healthcare Workers
research_question: To evaluate the effectiveness of multisensory, nature-inspired Recharge Rooms in reducing perceived stress among frontline healthcare workers during the COVID-19 pandemic.

participants.description: Frontline healthcare workers in a New York City hospital during the initial 2020 surge of SARS-CoV-2 cases.
participants.recruitment: Invited to book 15-min recharge experiences online via a website curated by the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai's Office of Resilience and Well-being.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Custom-designed 'Recharge Rooms' created by repurposing a 179.38 square foot neurophysiology laboratory. The rooms provided multisensory, nature-inspired experiences including silk imitation plants, projected scenes of soothing natural landscapes, low lighting tailored in color to match projected landscapes, high definition audio recordings of nature sounds paired with relaxing music, and an infusion of essential oils (yuzu, hinoki, roman chamomile, lavender) using an essential oil diffuser. The experience was voice-activated via Google Home.

measures.instrument: Single-item Likert-style measure (1-6 scale, 1=Not stressed at all, 6=Extremely stressed)
Single-item Likert-style measure (1-6 scale, 1=Not stressed at all, 6=Extremely stressed)
Net Promoter Score (NPS) (0-10 scale, 0=Not at all willing, 10=Very willing)

findings.quote: Prior to entry into the Recharge Room, average stress level was reported as 4.6/6 (±1.1).

findings.mechanism: soft fascination, stress relief and relaxation
findings.quote: After a single 15-min experience in the Recharge Room, the average user-reported stress level was significantly reduced 1.85/6 (±1.2; p < 0.001; paired t-test).
representing an average 59.6% reduction in self-reported stress levels
Net Promoter Score for the experience was 99.3%.
with 100% of respondents identifying as “promoters” (scores ranging between 8 and 10) of the experience.
These qualitative comments were universally positive, such as 'This is wonderful!' or 'This is such a needed and appreciated space at this time.'

mechanisms: creating moments of stress relief and relaxation
implementation_implications: Recharge Rooms produce significant short-term reductions in perceived stress.
Recharge Rooms are highly enjoyable for users.
These rooms may be of general utility in high-stress healthcare environments.

tables.description: User experience questionnaire characteristics, listing the questions, lower anchors, and upper anchors for the perceived stress and recommendation measures.

limitations: The program evaluation project lacks the rigor of a structured clinical trial.
The use of a single-item self-report state stress measures as opposed to well-validated measures of burnout.
The maintenance of stress reduction effects requires further investigation.
Limitations in how much the Net Promoter Score (NPS) short form can measure.
Results may not generalize to healthcare worker stress and anxiety experienced absent a global pandemic.

paper_metadata.title: Multisensory, Nature-Inspired Recharge Rooms Yield Short-Term Reductions in Perceived Stress Among Frontline Healthcare Workers
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Multisensory, Nature-Inspired Recharge Rooms Yield Short-Term Reductions in Perceived Stress Among Frontline Healthcare Workers
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: We are currently facing global healthcare crisis that has placed unprecedented stress on healthcare workers as a result of the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19). It is imperative that we develop novel tools to assist healthcare workers in dealing with the significant additional stress and trauma that has arisen as a result of the pandemic. Based in research on the effects of immersive environments on mood, a neuroscience research laboratory was rapidly repurposed using commercially available technologies and materials to create a nature-inspired relaxation space. Frontline healthcare workers were invited to book 15-min experiences in the Recharge Room before, during or after their shifts, where they were exposed to the immersive, multisensory experience 496 Recharge Room users (out of a total of 562) completed a short survey about their experience during an unselected, consecutive 14-day period. Average self-reported stress levels prior to entering the Recharge Room were 4.58/6 (±1.1). After a single 15-min experience in the Recharge Room, the average user-reported stress level was significantly reduced 1.85/6 (±1.2; p &lt; 0.001; paired t-test). Net Promoter Score for the experience was 99.3%. Recharge Rooms such as those described here produce significant short-term reductions in perceived stress, and users find them highly enjoyable. These rooms may be of general utility in high-stress healthcare environments.
